items.simple_meaning: To call someone is to talk to them using a phone.
items.explanation: When you call someone, you use a phone so you can hear their voice and talk, even if they are far away.
items.example_sentence: On Diwali morning, I call my grandmother to wish her a happy festival.
items.real_world_usage: Mummy, can we call Nani on the phone today?
items.spelling_guidance: Call ends with a double 'l' — c-a-l-l.
items.learning_objective: Children will use 'call' to describe talking to someone on a phone.
items.illustration_brief: A smiling child at home holding a phone to their ear, with a small picture bubble showing a happy grandmother talking back.

items.simple_meaning: A video is a recording of moving pictures, often with sound.
items.explanation: A video shows things moving, like a short film. You can watch a video on a television, computer or phone.
items.example_sentence: Our teacher showed us a video about how butterflies grow.
items.real_world_usage: Papa, can we watch the video of my school sports day again?
items.spelling_guidance: Video has two vowel sounds at the end: v-i-d-e-o.
items.learning_objective: Children will identify a video as moving pictures they can watch and talk about.
items.illustration_brief: A classroom where children sit together watching a screen that shows a colourful butterfly coming out of a cocoon.

items.simple_meaning: A website is a group of pages you can look at on the internet.
items.explanation: A website has pages with words, pictures and games that you open on a computer, tablet or phone. Each website has its own name and address.
items.example_sentence: My sister and I looked at a website about animals to finish our school project.
items.real_world_usage: Didi, can you open the website with the space pictures?
items.spelling_guidance: Website is two small words joined together: web + site.
items.learning_objective: Children will understand that a website is a set of pages on the internet that they visit with an adult's help.
items.illustration_brief: A child and a parent sitting together at a computer showing a bright page with pictures of animals, with no readable text.

items.simple_meaning: Straight means going in one direction without turning.
items.explanation: If you go straight, you keep walking forward and do not turn left or right. It helps you give and follow directions to a place.
items.example_sentence: To reach the school gate, walk straight past the big neem tree.
items.real_world_usage: Go straight down the road and the park is right there.
items.spelling_guidance: Straight has a silent 'gh' in the middle: s-t-r-a-i-g-h-t.
items.learning_objective: Children will use 'straight' to give and follow simple directions to places.
items.illustration_brief: A long road with an arrow pointing forward, a child walking ahead past a big tree towards a school gate.

items.simple_meaning: To drop something is to let it fall.
items.explanation: When you drop something, it slips out of your hand and falls down. Sometimes we drop things by mistake.
items.example_sentence: Be careful not to drop your tiffin box on the way to school.
items.real_world_usage: Oops, I drop my pencil every time I laugh!
items.spelling_guidance: When you add -ed or -ing, double the 'p': dropped, dropping.
items.learning_objective: Children will use 'drop' to describe letting something fall.
items.illustration_brief: A child with a surprised face as a tiffin box slips from their hands towards the ground, with motion lines showing it falling.

items.simple_meaning: To hurt means to feel pain in a part of your body.
items.explanation: When something hurts, it feels sore or painful. If you get hurt, tell a grown-up so they can help you feel better.
items.example_sentence: My knee began to hurt after I slipped while playing cricket, so Papa put a bandage on it.
items.real_world_usage: Ma'am, my finger hurts — can you help me?
items.spelling_guidance: Hurt is spelt with 'ur' like in 'turn' and 'burn'.
items.learning_objective: Children will use 'hurt' to tell an adult when a part of their body feels pain.
items.illustration_brief: A child sitting on a step while a caring parent gently puts a bandage on their knee, with a cricket bat nearby.

items.simple_meaning: A library is a place where you can read and borrow books.
items.explanation: A library has many shelves full of books. You can read there quietly or take a book home and bring it back later.
items.example_sentence: Every Friday, our class goes to the school library to choose a new storybook.
items.real_world_usage: I want to borrow a book about dinosaurs from the library.
items.spelling_guidance: Don't forget the first 'r': li-brar-y, not 'libary'.
items.learning_objective: Children will recognise a library as a place to read and borrow books.
items.illustration_brief: A bright school library with tall colourful bookshelves and children sitting on mats happily reading books.

items.simple_meaning: A holiday is a time when you do not go to school or work, often to travel or rest.
items.explanation: During a holiday, families may visit new places, see relatives or just relax. Summer holidays are a fun break from school.
items.example_sentence: During the summer holiday, we took a train to visit my cousins in the hills.
items.real_world_usage: We are going to the beach on holiday next week!
items.learning_objective: Children will use 'holiday' to talk about a break from school and family trips.
items.illustration_brief: A family with suitcases looking out of a train window at green hills, with smiling faces.

items.simple_meaning: Temperature is how hot or cold something is.
items.explanation: We use temperature to tell how hot or cold the weather is. A thermometer measures the temperature.
items.example_sentence: In May, the temperature gets very high, so we drink lots of water.
items.real_world_usage: The temperature is so cold today that I need my sweater.
items.spelling_guidance: Break it into parts: tem-per-a-ture, and remember the 'a' in the middle.
items.learning_objective: Children will use 'temperature' to describe how hot or cold the weather is.
items.illustration_brief: A large outdoor thermometer beside a sunny scene on one side and a chilly winter scene on the other.

items.simple_meaning: A comic is a book or story told with pictures in boxes and speech bubbles.
items.explanation: A comic tells a story using drawings in small boxes. The characters talk in speech bubbles.
items.example_sentence: After finishing my homework, I read a funny comic about a clever monkey.
items.real_world_usage: Can I draw my own comic about our cricket match?
items.spelling_guidance: Comic ends with 'ic', just like 'music' and 'picnic'.
items.learning_objective: Children will recognise a comic as a story told with pictures and speech bubbles.
items.illustration_brief: A child sitting on a bed reading an open comic book with colourful picture boxes and empty speech bubbles showing a cheerful monkey.
